At the garment factory, each sewing line has a screen that shows its output against the hourly target in red or green. Supervisors walk behind the women but rarely speak; the screen speaks for them. During the afternoon shift, Shapla's line falls into red. The women do not complain. Instead, at exactly 4 p.m., all twelve go to the toilet together, "because we are sisters". The line stays red for ten minutes. The supervisor writes nothing down. The next morning, the target on the screen has been lowered slightly.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a garment factory in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

In the village in Kerala, the new houses have two storeys, marble floors and gates painted gold. Locals call them "Gulf houses". Many stand empty for eleven months of the year while their owners work in Dubai and Doha. Leela, whose husband has worked in Qatar for fifteen years, manages the money, the children's schooling and the land. "In the beginning I asked his mother for everything," she says. "Now the bank knows my name." When her husband returns each summer, he asks her how to pay the electricity bill online.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Kerala, India.

Explain, with close reference to the text, how migration has changed gender and household relations in the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Remittances transform the material landscape (Gulf houses as status symbols), while the husband's long absence shifts authority to Leela: she gains financial autonomy, independence from her mother-in-law and new competences, reversing knowledge roles with her husband – an example of migration reorganising households and gender relations transnationally.

At Gate 32 of the airport, the cleaners have their own map. Esperanza shows me "the corner of the Filipinos", a row of seats near a power socket where colleagues eat lunch, and "the chapel", a disused smoking room where two Muslim cleaners pray. Last month, management removed the seats near the socket to "improve passenger flow".

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Ong's Flexible Citizenship and Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus, compare and contrast the role of power in borders, citizenship and the state's control of movement.
items.answer: Ong's Flexible Citizenship (among wealthy Chinese business families moving between Hong Kong, South-East Asia and North America (1990s)): States court wealthy migrants with investor visas while restricting poorer ones, so the ability to move and belong is unequally distributed. Mukamana, a survivor, sits at the front; three rows behind her sits Jean-Paul, who served his sentence for taking part in the killings and now farms the next field. For two years I volunteered at the night shelter, where I also conducted my research. Most residents knew me as "the student who helps". Pete, who has been sleeping rough for eight years, told me about selling his medication to buy alcohol, then added, "But that's just between us." items.stem: Compare and contrast Malkki's Purity and Exile and Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus as accounts of belonging, home and identity among mobile and displaced people, focusing on the key concept of belonging.
items.answer: Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): Camp refugees saw exile as a moral trial and Burundi as the homeland to which they truly belonged; town refugees sought to belong locally. Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus (in Kahnawà:ke, a Mohawk community near Montreal, Canada): Community membership rules are debated as Mohawks decide who belongs in the face of colonial definitions imposed by the Indian Act. items.stem: Using Sanday's Women at the Center (among the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia (fieldwork from 1981)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: Sanday calls the Minangkabau a "matriarchy" in the sense that women are at the symbolic and social centre, controlling ancestral houses and land, without ruling over men.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Sanday calls the Minangkabau a "matriarchy" in the sense that women are at the symbolic and social centre, controlling ancestral houses and land, without ruling over men. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Peggy Reeves Sanday, Women at the Center: Life in a Modern Matriarchy (2002), among the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia (fieldwork from 1981)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Strathern's The Gender of the Gift and Kahn's Reproducing Jews, compare and contrast the role of identity in new kinship, chosen kin and reproductive technologies.
items.answer: Strathern's The Gender of the Gift (drawing on her fieldwork in Mount Hagen, Papua New Guinea, and Melanesian ethnography): Strathern argues that Melanesian persons are "dividuals" composed of relationships, and that gender is a quality of acts and objects in exchange rather than a fixed attribute of bodies. Kahn's Reproducing Jews (among unmarried women, clinicians and rabbis in Israel (fieldwork 1990s)): Reproductive technologies were embraced in Israel partly because having children is seen as a religious and national duty. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far identity is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Explain how the Why We Post project illustrates the concept of change. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values. items.stem: Using Hodgson's Once Intrepid Warriors and Tsing's Friction, compare the ways in which change is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Hodgson's Once Intrepid Warriors (among Maasai pastoralists in northern Tanzania): Development schemes, loss of land and market integration transformed pastoral livelihoods and gender relations. Tsing's Friction (in the Meratus Mountains of South Kalimantan, Indonesia, and among Indonesian environmental activists): Global connections such as logging, environmentalism and investment produce "friction" – awkward, unequal encounters that generate new cultural forms. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far change is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
